newsitem.title: GERMANY: INSTANT VIEW - German April unemployment data.
newsitem.headline: INSTANT VIEW - German April unemployment data.

text.p: Following are reactions of economists to German unemployment data, which showed a slight seasonally-adjusted rise to 4.299 million in April. The unemployment rate, which is based on unadjusted data, fell to 11.3 percent, compared with 11.7 percent in March.

"This is a disappointment, it shows that the trend in seasonally-unadjusted unemployment is still upwards. Further seasonally-adjusted rises are to be expected up until the autumn, when we can expect a bottoming out."

CHRISTIAN SOBOTTA, LGT Asset Management: "The 8,000 increase is very disappointing, indicating that seasonally-adjusted figures are still rising. It looks as if we are going to have to get used to unemployment in the double-digit percent category.

"The (previously-released) industrial production figures were pretty good, leading us to expect a first-quarter gross domestic product rise at close to three percent. We are achieving gains in production but no increases in employment -- this may be good for the stock market, but it is not good for the labour market and possibly not good (for the government) in terms of the polls.

Referring to the value of the mark, Sobotta added however that at some point "the Bundesbank can still be expected to increase interest rates, so I think we shall see the dollar coming down to 1.70 or 1.65 marks after having earlier gone up to as much as 1.75 to 1.78 marks."

HANS GUENTER REDEKER, CHASE INVESTMENTS: "If you get productivity gains (as Germany is), unemployment has to rise. The figures are in line with our expectations and will put more pressure on the government, throwing their forecast for a 2.9 pct (ratio of 1997 budget deficit to gross domestic product) yet further open to question. The next crucial data will be the tax estimation for this year (due this month). We expect a shortfall of 12-14 billion marks compared to the autumn release. Even a ratio just over 3.0 percent will require further consolidation".
